strengths: The paper identifies a useful distinction between explaining predictions through raw inputs and through interpretable concepts, where omitted concepts can introduce confounding. This has an identifiable audience in causal discovery, explainability, and model auditing.

Applying FCI with the background knowledge that predictions cannot cause image features is well motivated under the stated causal assumptions. PAGs appropriately represent unresolved causal relationships, and this application of established methods can be informative without requiring a new algorithm.

The presentation clearly motivates type-level causal explanation, specifies a structural causal model, and explains graphical notation. Sections 7.2–7.3 usefully acknowledge limits from identifiability, background knowledge, and feature selection.

The omitted-feature simulation provides a focused illustration, while the bird and X-ray applications make the workflow concrete. The appendices provide useful preprocessing and implementation details.
weaknesses: Necessary: Preserve the distinction between possible causation and established causation throughout the results. Section 6.3 pools directed and partially directed edges; high frequency of a partially directed edge remains compatible with pure confounding. Furthermore, absence of adjacency to the prediction does not exclude mediated causation. Figure 10 permits Cardiomegaly to affect the prediction through Atelectasis, despite its zero direct-edge stability in Figure 8. Claims that other features are not causally relevant therefore exceed the analysis. Report edge types separately and account for possible ancestral paths.

Necessary: Address selection in the X-ray experiment. Selecting pneumonia cases and controls with no findings makes inclusion depend on disease status and explanatory features. Such selection can induce dependencies and affect the ancestral interpretations used by the proposed analysis. Section 3's assertion that selection bias is irrelevant is consequently unjustified for this application. Explicitly account for the sampling mechanism, justify why it preserves the relevant conclusions, or withdraw the corresponding causal interpretations.

Necessary: Correct Example 1 and Appendix A.2. The purported adjustment with Z3 omitted keeps Z3 fixed inside f'(Z1,Z2,Z3). An observed-data backdoor calculation using only Z2 instead requires E[Yhat | Z1,Z2], which integrates over the conditional distribution of the unobserved Z3. The displayed zero-attribution formula therefore does not establish the claimed failure of that procedure. Define the coalition values consistently and recompute the comparison; a zero local attribution also should not itself be equated with type-level causal irrelevance.

Necessary: The reliability of the real-data independence tests is insufficiently established. Chi-square tests with 26 multivalued bird attributes and conditioning sets of up to four variables can produce very sparse contingency tables; the X-ray analysis has only 240 images. Bootstrap stability does not establish test calibration or causal correctness. Clarify which data splits supply FCI observations and demonstrate that the tests supporting the key orientations are reliable, with appropriate sensitivity checks. Otherwise, present the empirical findings as exploratory hypotheses. Clinical or ornithological plausibility alone does not validate the inferred causes.

Optional: A comparison using the same annotated features, such as an associational ranking or a causal discovery method assuming causal sufficiency, would better isolate the benefit of handling latent confounding. The LIME/SHAP examples mainly illustrate differences in representation and explanatory target. Repeated simulations with controlled feature interventions would also strengthen evidence about recovery reliability.
